newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba rates seen steady next week but rising soon.
newsitem.headline: Buba rates seen steady next week but rising soon.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank will not raise interest rates next week but has prepared markets for a rise in the coming months, mainly because it wants to ensure a stable single European currency, analysts said on Friday.

The Bundesbank's recent warnings of inflationary pressures in Germany are a pretext which has worked neatly to stem the mark's weakening against the dollar by provoking fears of an interest rate rise, the analysts said.

Four of five economists asked by Reuters said they did not expect a rate rise next week, either on Tuesday when the next auction for securities repurchase agreements (repos) is set or on Thursday when the Bundesbank council reconvenes after a four-week summer break.
But several economists said they expected the Bundesbank's main money market rate, the repo rate, to rise by end-1997, with a move possible in the next six weeks.
Forecasts for a rise in the repo rate range between 20 and 50 basis points by the end of the year.
At 3.00 percent, Germany's repo rate is too low to be the norm for European short-term rates once monetary union is launched in 1999, especially if it starts with a large group of members.
Economists say the Bundesbank is aware it must act soon to avoid upsetting markets with sudden rate increases as monetary union, scheduled to be launched in in 1999, draws closer.
That is why the bank spent its summer recess sending clear signals to financial markets that the next interest rate move will be up, and giving itself scope to act at short notice.

Economists said the policy has helped prevent the strengthening dollar from getting out of control. The U.S. unit has weakened by five pfennigs against the mark in the past week and was trading at 1.8350 marks at 1230 GMT on Friday.
"The Bundesbank is keeping a sword hanging over the market. It can achieve more with the threat of action than with action itself," said Ulrich Beckmann at Deutsche Bank Research.

The latest warning came from Bundesbank deputy president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum who said in a newspaper interview on Friday the bank was concerned about domestic price pressures in the pipeline and that it wanted "full scope to act."
Gaddum gave a strong indication that the Bundesbank had departed from its policy of announcing terms of forthcoming weekly repo auctions after each fortnightly council meeting.

The market's certainty is over since the Bundesbank at its last meeting before its summer break announced the repo terms for just two weeks, leaving markets in the dark about this week's and next week's repos.
Markets are now likely to be kept guessing about possible repo changes each Tuesday when the bank sets its weekly repo auction.
"As regards our decisions we have to operate in a more uncertain environment and therefore want to retain full leeway in our Tuesday allocations," Gaddum told Handelsblatt.
Economists see the Bundesbank's inflation warning as an excuse to justify a rate increase.

While the mark's slide of about 20 percent against the dollar is bound to fuel import price gains, the impact on consumer prices will be easily offset by Germany's high unemployment, weak consumer spending and low unit labour costs.

"If the Bundesbank raises rates they'll do it for EMU reasons. It's clear that a euro with broad membership can't start with short-term rates at 2.50 percent," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at UBS in Frankfurt.
The Bundesbank's discount rate, which sets the floor for German money market rates, is 2.50 percent. The repo rate has been fixed at 3.00 percent for the past 12 months.
Gerhard Grebe, an economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, sees the repo rate at 3.25 percent by end-1997 and at 3.50 percent in early 1998, when EMU members will be chosen.

He sees the discount rate rising by 50 basis points to three percent in the first quarter of 1998, and expects the Lombard rate, which forms the ceiling to German money market rates, to rise to five percent from 4.5 percent.
Meanwhile July data for M3 money supply, the Bundesbank's main policy indicator, are due next week and may dampen expectations of an imminent interest rate rise.
Economists polled by Reuters on average expect M3 growth to have slowed marginally to 6.3 percent from 6.4 percent in June.
The Ifo institute's business sentiment index for July is expected to rise to 96.6 from 96.00, the fourth monthly rise in a row.
